1366.title: One Buddha or many
1366.hook: the historical Buddha, and the many Buddhas of the Mahayana
1366.howItsDone: Theravada Buddhists honor Gotama, the Buddha of this age, at temple and home shrines, while Mahayana Buddhists also honor other Buddhas, such as Amitabha in Pure Land practice and the Medicine Buddha.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bodhisattva: the vow to free all beings, and two ideals, each honored in its own home. Your line was both honored.

Two altars. On the first, in a village temple in Sri Lanka, one seated figure: a man who walked the dusty roads of northern India, ate what was put in his bowl, grew old, fell ill, and died among his friends. On the second, in a temple in Kyoto, a golden Buddha with his hand raised, and behind him a painted sky crowded with more Buddhas than anyone could count, each with a world of its own. Same word on both altars: Buddha. Two pictures of who that is, and how many.
screen: `A VILLAGE ALTAR: ONE MAN.` → `A KYOTO ALTAR: A SKY OF BUDDHAS.` → `SAME WORD.`

segments.voice: First, the one. In the Pali texts, the Buddha of our age is Gotama: a teacher with a body that aches, who tells Ananda near the end that he is like an old cart held together with straps. His last words, in Rhys Davids's translation, are plain and human: "Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!" The Theravada honors that one teacher, gone into final nibbana, and the teaching that remains. Second, even the Pali texts look backward and forward. A long discourse names Buddhas who came before Gotama, in ages long past, and another speaks of Metteyya, a Buddha still to come. One Buddha for an age; many across time. Third, the many. Mahayana sutras widen the picture into space. Amitabha, the Buddha of boundless light, presides over a pure land in the west, and Pure Land Buddhists call on his name. The Medicine Buddha heals in a land of lapis light. Vairocana shines at the center of the cosmos in Japanese and Chinese temples. And the Lotus Sutra adds a startling turn: the Buddha who seemed to be born, awaken and die, it says, actually awakened ages beyond measure ago, and showed a death as a teaching device so people would not grow careless. Fourth, how each holds it. For the Theravada, honoring one teacher who truly walked and truly died is the heart of devotion. For the Mahayana schools that hold it, the vast picture shows how wide awakening is.

Then let the picture open, like a camera pulling back to the night sky, light upon light, world upon world. You don't need to choose; let each be what it is for those who hold it.
One Buddha or many. The Buddha of our age, Gotama, honored as one teacher who lived and died; and the many Buddhas across time and space in the Mahayana. Today's word.
Your line: one and many. Each school explains its own altar. Go gently.

1367.title: Buddha-nature views
1367.hook: some schools teach inborn Buddha-nature; others speak of what can be developed
1367.howItsDone: In Zen, students may work with the koan of Zhaozhou's dog for a long time with a teacher; Theravada practitioners speak of cultivating the perfections, and Tibetan monastic colleges study and debate the nature of Buddha-nature.

segments.voice: Yesterday, one Buddha or many: one teacher on a dusty road, and a sky full of Buddhas. Your line was one and many.

A monk comes to the old Chinese teacher Zhaozhou, whom you met over tea in year three, with what sounds like an easy question. The sutras say every living being has Buddha-nature. So does a dog have Buddha-nature? Zhaozhou answers with one syllable. Wu. No. Nothing. Zen students still sit with that single word, turning it over until something gives. Why would a teacher who knew the sutras say no? Hold on to that.
screen: `DOES A DOG HAVE BUDDHA-NATURE?` → `WU.` → `BORN, OR GROWN?`

segments.voice: First, the inborn view. A group of Mahayana scriptures, among them the Mahaparinirvana Sutra, teach that all beings have Buddha-nature, sometimes called the tathagatagarbha, the womb or seed of a Buddha. Awakening isn't built from scratch. It's already there, covered over like gold in the earth or a jewel sewn into a beggar's coat, and practice uncovers it. Zen and other schools of East Asia grew up with this teaching. Second, the koan. So why does Zhaozhou say no? Zen teachers say Wu isn't a doctrine to agree or disagree with. It's a gate. Holding Buddha-nature as an idea can become one more thing to cling to, and Wu cuts the rope. Third, the developmental view. The Theravada speaks less of a hidden Buddha inside and more of qualities to be grown: generosity, ethics, patience, wisdom, the perfections cultivated over a long path. The Pali texts do have a striking line: the Anguttara Nikaya says the mind is luminous, stained by defilements that arrive from outside. Some teachers take that as a seed of the inborn view; others read it simply as a reason to practice. Fourth, voices within one tradition. Tibetan schools debate this too. Some say Buddha-nature is the mind's emptiness, which makes growth possible; others, a radiant nature with qualities already complete. Each explains itself carefully. And some teachers say a practitioner needs both: trust that it's there, and effort to grow it.

segments.voice: For the first minute, rest as if there's nothing to add, as if the clear, kind mind is already here under the noise, like sky behind clouds. For the second, choose one quality to grow, patience perhaps, or generosity, and breathe as if you're watering a seed. There's no need to decide which minute was right.
Buddha-nature views. Some schools teach that awakening is already present in every being, waiting to be uncovered; others speak of qualities grown on the path. Today's word.
Your line: born or grown. A seed to trust, and a seed to water. See you tomorrow.

1368.title: Emptiness in each school
1368.hook: not-self in the Pali texts, emptiness in the Mahayana: related, differently stressed
1368.howItsDone: Theravada practitioners contemplate not-self in the body and mind during insight meditation, while Mahayana communities often chant the Heart Sutra and study emptiness through Nagarjuna's writings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Buddha-nature: the seed already there, the qualities grown, and Zhaozhou's Wu. Your line was born or grown.

Ananda, the Buddha's attendant, asks him a plain question in the Pali texts. People say the world is empty. In what way is it empty? It's the kind of question a friend asks on a long walk, and the Buddha gives a plain answer: the world is empty of a self, and of anything belonging to a self. The eye, the forms it sees, the thoughts that follow: none of them is a self you could own. Later, Mahayana teachers would build a great deal on that one word, empty.
screen: `EMPTY OF WHAT?` → `EMPTY OF A SELF.` → `WHERE EACH PUTS THE WEIGHT.`

segments.voice: First, not-self in the Pali texts, which you met back in year one. In one talk, the Buddha takes the body, feelings, perceptions, mental formations and consciousness one at a time. If the body were a self, he says, it wouldn't lead to affliction; you could tell it, let my body be this way, and it would obey. It doesn't. So it isn't a self. The Pali word is anatta. The weight falls on persons: the bundle you call me, seen through, so clinging loosens. Second, emptiness in the Mahayana. The Perfection of Wisdom sutras, and the short one people chant, the Heart Sutra, widen the word: not just the person but every thing, every quality, even the teachings themselves, are empty of a fixed, independent nature. One line, in paraphrase: form is emptiness, and emptiness is form. Third, Nagarjuna's turn. The Indian teacher Nagarjuna said that emptiness is simply dependent arising: things are empty because they come from causes and conditions, not because they don't exist at all. Emptiness, he warned, is not a new thing to grab. Fourth, the stress. Theravada teachers also speak of all phenomena as not-self, and Mahayana teachers also teach not-self of the person. Same root, both sides. What differs is where the weight lands: the person seen through, or everything seen through, including the seeing.

segments.voice: Wait for one sound to arrive, a car, a bird, the hum of a fridge, and as it comes and goes, note gently, the old Pali way: this is not mine to command. Then, the Mahayana way, notice what the same sound leans on, air, ears, distance, attention, and let it be empty of standing alone. Notice one difference between the two, kindly, without crowning either.
Emptiness in each school. Not-self of the person in the Pali texts; the emptiness of all things in the Mahayana. Related teachings, differently stressed. Today's word.
Your line: differently stressed. Two ways of seeing through, one root beneath them. Until tomorrow.

1369.title: Views of rebirth
1369.hook: most schools teach rebirth; some modern practitioners stay agnostic; each gives its reasons
1369.howItsDone: Classical Buddhist schools teach rebirth as a continuing stream of causes shaped by karma, and Tibetan Buddhists recognize reborn teachers; some modern practitioners hold the question open and practice for this life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, emptiness in each school: not-self in the Pali texts, the emptiness of all things in the Mahayana. Your line was differently stressed.

A king named Milinda puts a sharp question to a monk named Nagasena. If there's no lasting self, who is reborn? The same person, or someone else? Nagasena answers with a lamp. Light one lamp from another. Is it the same flame? Not quite. A different flame? Not quite either. The second depends on the first. The king, the text says, is satisfied. It's an old question, asked honestly, and the schools have kept asking it.
screen: `WHO IS REBORN?` → `ONE LAMP LIGHTS ANOTHER.` → `NOT THE SAME, NOT DIFFERENT.`

segments.voice: First, the classical teaching. In the Pali texts, on the night of his awakening, the Buddha recalls his own former lives, then sees beings passing away and arising again according to their actions. Rebirth here is not a soul moving house. It's a stream of causes, like the flame passing from lamp to lamp. Theravada, Mahayana and Tibetan teachers have taught it this way through their classic texts, and in Tibet it shapes the practice of recognizing reborn teachers. Second, the reasons given. Teachers point to the Buddha's own account, to the logic of karma, that actions have results that don't stop at death, and to the sense that a moral universe hangs together. These are reasons offered for testing, not commands. Third, the agnostic voice. Some modern practitioners say they don't know whether rebirth happens, and practice for what they can see in this life. They give reasons too: honesty about what they can know, and the Buddha's warning against clinging to views. Fourth, a teaching that holds the question open: the Kalama Sutta, which you met in year one, where the Buddha speaks to villagers confused by rival teachers. He describes a person whose mind is free of hatred and ill will, and the comforts that person has. If there is a world beyond, and fruit of good and bad deeds, I'll arrive well. If there isn't, then here and now I live free of hatred, at ease. Either way, the same life.
screen: `THE NIGHT OF AWAKENING: FORMER LIVES.` · `REASONS: THE ACCOUNT, KARMA, ORDER.` · `SOME MODERN PRACTITIONERS: WE DON'T KNOW.` · `THE KALAMA SUTTA: EITHER WAY.` · then, large: `HELD HONESTLY.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself quietly what you actually think about rebirth, not what you're supposed to think: yes, no, or I don't know. Then try the Kalama Sutta's turn: whichever is true, what would a life free of ill will look like today? Let the question stay open if it's open.
Views of rebirth. The classical teaching of a stream of causes continuing, life to life; and the modern practitioners who hold it open. Each gives its reasons. Today's word.
Your line: held honestly. Each school gives its reasons, and the question can stay open. That's today, done.

1370.title: Lay and monastic
1370.hook: some schools center the monastery, others the household
1370.howItsDone: In Theravada countries lay people offer food to monks on the morning alms round and receive teaching and blessings in return; in Japanese Jodo Shinshu, married priests often lead temples, and householders practice at home.

segments.voice: Yesterday, views of rebirth: Nagasena's lamp, and the Kalama Sutta's either way. Your line was held honestly.

First light, a quiet street in Laos. A line of monks in orange robes walks barefoot, bowls held in front of them. Along the curb, people kneel on mats with baskets of sticky rice still warm from the steamer. A pinch of rice into each bowl. No one speaks. The monks don't ask. At the end, a short chant of blessing from the monks to the people who gave. Two kinds of life, meeting on one sidewalk at dawn, each feeding the other.
screen: `DAWN IN LAOS: THE ALMS ROUND.` → `RICE INTO THE BOWL.` → `A BLESSING BACK.`

segments.voice: First, the monastery at the center. In Theravada lands, the sangha of monks and nuns keeps the full discipline, studies and meditates, and depends on lay people for food, robes and medicine. In return, monks give the teaching and blessings. It's an exchange, not charity in one direction. Second, the householder in the old texts. The Pali canon honors lay disciples by name: Anathapindika, the merchant who bought a park to give to the Buddha; Visakha, the generous laywoman; and Citta, a householder so learned that, in one discourse, he explains a fine point of the teaching to monks. In the Sigalovada Sutta, the Buddha gives a young householder a whole ethic of family life: parents and children, teachers and students, friends, workers. Third, the household at the center. In Japan, Shinran, of the Pure Land school, whom you met in year three, married and raised a family, and described himself as neither monk nor layman. The Jodo Shinshu temples that followed him are often led by married priests and their families. In Tibet, some householder yogis, called ngakpas, keep tantric vows while raising children and farming. Fourth, the layman who outtalks everyone. In the Vimalakirti Sutra, a wealthy householder falls ill, and the great disciples and bodhisattvas are each reluctant to visit, because he has bested them all in debate. When the question of non-duality finally comes, Vimalakirti answers with silence, and the sutra praises that silence. Some schools center the monastery, others the household, and each gives its reasons.
screen: `THE MONASTERY: AN EXCHANGE.` · `CITTA, ANATHAPINDIKA, VISAKHA.` · `SHINRAN: NEITHER MONK NOR LAYMAN.` · `VIMALAKIRTI'S SILENCE.` · then, large: `TWO LIVES.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who gave up a household for a life of practice, a monk, a nun, anyone who chose simplicity, and breathe with gratitude for what their choice keeps alive. 1371.title: Devotion and meditation
1371.hook: chanting the name and silent sitting: both are practice
1371.howItsDone: Pure Land Buddhists recite the name of Amitabha (Amituofo, Namu Amida Butsu); Zen practitioners sit in silent meditation; Theravada Buddhists chant the recollection of the Buddha's qualities; and some temples hold both chanting and sitting.

segments.voice: Yesterday, lay and monastic: rice into the bowl at first light, Shinran's household, Vimalakirti's silence. Your line was two lives.

Which room in a temple is doing the real practice? Take an evening in a Chinese temple. In the main hall, a room full of voices chants one name over and over, Amituofo, Amituofo, steady as rain on a roof. Walk across the courtyard to the meditation hall and there's nothing. A robe rustles. Someone's knee cracks. A clock ticks. Same temple, same hour, two completely different sounds. The temple's answer: the question is a little off.
screen: `AMITUOFO, STEADY AS RAIN.` → `ACROSS THE COURTYARD: SILENCE.` → `WHICH ROOM IS PRACTICING?`

segments.voice: First, devotion inside the Pali texts. In a Pali discourse, the Buddha tells monks meditating alone in the forest that if fear rises in them, they should recollect him: the Blessed One, worthy, fully awakened, perfect in knowledge and conduct. Recollecting the Buddha's qualities, buddhanussati, is a meditation in the Theravada, and also an act of devotion. The line between the two is thin from the start. Second, the name. In Pure Land Buddhism, practitioners call on the name of Amitabha, Amida in Japanese. In Japan, Honen taught the nembutsu, Namu Amida Butsu, as the practice for ordinary people; for him, the name chanted aloud was path enough. His student Shinran taught it as gratitude for a gift already given. Third, the silence. In the Soto Zen school, Dogen taught shikantaza, just sitting: no name, no object, nothing to get. Upright and awake, the sitting itself is the practice. Fourth, the two joined. Some Chinese teachers combined them: recite the Buddha's name with the whole heart, then turn and ask, who is reciting? The chant opens into a question, and the question into silence. In Tibet, people turn prayer wheels and chant mantras, then sit in stillness on the same cushion. Some schools lean on the voice, some on silence, and each explains itself.
screen: `RECOLLECTING THE BUDDHA, IN THE FOREST.` · `NAMU AMIDA BUTSU: THE NAME.` · `SHIKANTAZA: JUST SITTING.` · `WHO IS RECITING?` · then, large: `BOTH ARE PRACTICE.`

segments.voice: For a minute, repeat a traditional phrase softly, aloud or in your head: Namo Buddhaya, homage to the Buddha, used in Theravada lands, or Namu Amida Butsu, the Japanese nembutsu; or simply recall the Buddha's qualities, awake, kind, clear. Then let the words fall away and sit, upright, breathing, with nothing to get.
Devotion and meditation. Calling the name and sitting in silence, recollecting the Buddha and just sitting: different schools lean different ways, and both are practice. Today's word.
Your line: both are practice. In some temples, the two halls share one courtyard. See you tomorrow.

1372.title: Sudden and gradual
1372.hook: schools stress sudden awakening or gradual training, and some hold both together
1372.howItsDone: Some Zen and Chan schools speak of sudden awakening and tell stories of breakthrough moments; Theravada teachers often describe a gradual training in stages; and teachers such as the Korean master Chinul taught sudden awakening followed by gradual cultivation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, devotion and meditation: a name chanted aloud, and a silence kept. Your line was both are practice.

Two verses are pinned to a monastery wall in old China, so the story goes. The abbot is choosing an heir, and has asked his monks to write down what they understand. The senior monk writes that the mind is like a bright mirror, and the work is to wipe it, again and again, so no dust can settle. People nod. Then a kitchen worker who cannot read asks someone to write a reply for him. The mirror, he says, was never a thing to begin with. So where would the dust land? One verse is about patient cleaning. The other is about seeing all at once.
screen: `TWO VERSES ON A WALL.` → `WIPE THE MIRROR.` → `WHAT MIRROR?`

segments.voice: That story comes from the Platform Sutra, which tells it about the senior monk Shenxiu and the kitchen worker Huineng. Chan tradition later spoke of a southern school that stressed sudden awakening and a northern school that stressed gradual training. The two words stuck. Now go back to the Pali texts, and both are already there. In one discourse, the Buddha compares his teaching to the great ocean, whose floor slopes down little by little, with no sudden cliff. So too the training is gradual, step by step; knowledge does not come in an abrupt leap. Then there is Bahiya of the bark cloth. He finds the Buddha on his alms round in the street and will not wait. The Buddha gives him a teaching of a few lines: in the seen, let there be only the seen; in the heard, only the heard. And right there, the text says, Bahiya's mind is freed. No years of training on the page. Just a street, and a sentence. So which is it? Some teachers would say the question is the wrong shape. The Korean teacher Chinul taught sudden awakening followed by gradual cultivation: you may see clearly in one moment, then spend years letting your habits catch up. Ice may be seen to be water at once, and still take time to melt. Zen halls tell stories of breakthroughs; Theravada teachers map the path in stages, as the ocean simile does. Each keeps the other side somewhere in its house.
screen: `SHENXIU AND HUINENG.` · `THE OCEAN SLOPES SLOWLY.` · `BAHIYA IN THE STREET.` · `SEE AT ONCE, THEN MELT.` · then, large: `BOTH ARE TRUE.`

segments.voice: Call up one insight that came suddenly, a moment when something just clicked, and stay with it for a few breaths. Then call up one that came slowly, a patience built over years, a habit that took countless small tries. One opened a door; the other walked you through it.
Sudden and gradual. Two ways schools describe awakening: seen in a flash, or grown by steady training, and often both, one after the other. Today's word.
Your line: both are true. The week closes: one Buddha or many, Buddha-nature, emptiness, rebirth, lay and monastic, devotion and meditation, and sudden and gradual. A full week, done.

chat.meaning: Both sides appear early: the Pali ocean floor slopes little by little, and Bahiya is freed in the street. Chinul joined them: see at once, then cultivate.
